I have been farming these 5 mu for forty years, and at sixty-eight I know what my wife and I can handle with just the two of us. The cabbage–longbean–spinach rotation on three mu is our bread and butter; it keeps the land busy and brings steady cash. I will plant three mu of hybrid spring cabbage first, rotary till the plots, and give it a good dose of fertilizer and four irrigations from the well. Once the cabbage comes off in early summer, I will put improved kidney bean seeds straight into the same beds, water it three times, and watch for pod borers. After the beans finish in autumn, I will sow improved spinach for the late-season crop. The other two mu I divide between one mu of hybrid chili and one mu of hybrid maize. The chili pays well at market but is fussy, so I will irrigate five times and spray four times to keep the fruit clean. The maize is for our own grain and feed; it is low-labor, so I will plough that plot, plant the hybrid seed, fertilize once, and water twice. I do not try no-tillage here because rotary tillage and ploughing give me the clean seedbeds I trust after decades of watching crops perform on this soil.

decision.reasoning_summary: With only two of us working and forty years of experience, I stick to the reliable cabbage–longbean–spinach rotation on three mu because it uses the land efficiently and gives three harvests a year. I use hybrid seeds for cabbage and chili to maximize income, and improved seeds for beans and spinach to balance cost and yield. The remaining two mu are split between chili for cash and maize for household grain and feed. I keep tillage simple—rotary for the vegetables and plough for maize—and irrigate according to what each crop actually needs from our well, never wasting water or labor.
